claim: The Drosophila melanogaster mushroom body has approximately 2000 Kenyon cells per hemisphere.
source: The mushroom body of each hemisphere has ~2000 Kenyon cells (KCs), which are two synapses from the sensory periphery.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the Introduction section providing a specific quantitative measurement of KC number.

claim: Each olfactory receptor neuron in adult Drosophila antennae expresses one or two of 75 olfactory receptor genes.
source: Each olfactory receptor neuron in the antennae of adult flies expresses one or two of 75 olfactory receptor genes encoded in the genome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the olfactory system organization in Drosophila.

claim: Axons of olfactory receptor neurons expressing the same receptor converge on one of 54 glomeruli in the antennal lobe.
source: The axons of neurons expressing the same receptor converge on one of 54 glomeruli in the antennal lobe.
evidence: This describes the established anatomical organization of the olfactory system.

claim: Approximately 150 uniglomerular projection neurons carry signals from the antennal lobe to the mushroom body calyx and lateral horn.
source: ~150 uniglomerular projection neurons (PNs) have dendrites in one of the 54 glomeruli and carry signals about distinct receptor channels to two regions of the protocerebrum, the lateral horn and the mushroom body calyx (Figure 1A).
evidence: This provides a quantitative description of the PN population with reference to a figure showing the anatomy.

claim: 90% of Kenyon cell inputs in Drosophila melanogaster are olfactory.
source: While mushroom bodies of different insect species process information from a variety of sensory modalities, 90% of Kenyon cell inputs in Drosophila melanogaster are olfactory (Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zheng et al., 2018.

claim: PN inputs to the lateral horn are thought to underlie innate behaviors.
source: PN inputs to the lateral horn are thought to underlie innate behaviors, while inputs to the mushroom body allow flexible learned association of odor stimuli with behavioral context (Chin et al., 2018; de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Fişek and Wilson, 2014; Jefferis et al., 2007; Ruta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the functional roles of different brain regions.

claim: PN inputs to the mushroom body allow flexible learned association of odor stimuli with behavioral context.
source: PN inputs to the lateral horn are thought to underlie innate behaviors, while inputs to the mushroom body allow flexible learned association of odor stimuli with behavioral context (Chin et al., 2018; de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Fişek and Wilson, 2014; Jefferis et al., 2007; Ruta et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the functional roles of the mushroom body.

claim: Each PN makes 1-20 boutons in the mushroom body calyx.
source: Each PN makes 1–20 boutons, and each bouton is wrapped by claws of ~10 KCs, such that each PN sends output to between 10 and 200 of the 2000 KCs (Leiss et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of PN bouton production supported by a citation.

claim: Each PN bouton is wrapped by claws of approximately 10 KCs.
source: Each PN makes 1–20 boutons, and each bouton is wrapped by claws of ~10 KCs, such that each PN sends output to between 10 and 200 of the 2000 KCs (Leiss et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the convergence ratio at individual boutons, supported by citation.

claim: Each PN sends output to between 10 and 200 of the 2000 KCs.
source: Each PN makes 1–20 boutons, and each bouton is wrapped by claws of ~10 KCs, such that each PN sends output to between 10 and 200 of the 2000 KCs (Leiss et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a calculation based on bouton number and KCs per bouton, supported by citation.

claim: KCs have 3-10 claws with an average of five.
source: KCs in turn have 3–10 (average of five) claws, which innervate boutons of various PNs (Caron et al., 2013; Gruntman and Turner, 2013; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This provides quantitative data on KC claw number supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each KC receives innervation from only a minority of the 54 incoming sensory channels.
source: Each KC therefore receives innervation from only a minority of the 54 incoming sensory channels, and different individual KCs receive different and relatively unstructured combinations of inputs (Caron et al., 2013; Eichler et al., 2017; Honegger et al., 2011; Murthy et al., 2008; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the sparse connectivity pattern, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Different individual KCs receive different and relatively unstructured combinations of inputs.
source: Each KC therefore receives innervation from only a minority of the 54 incoming sensory channels, and different individual KCs receive different and relatively unstructured combinations of inputs (Caron et al., 2013; Eichler et al., 2017; Honegger et al., 2011; Murthy et al., 2008; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the variability in KC input patterns, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The sets of inputs to individual KCs vary across hemispheres and likely across individuals.
source: The sets of inputs to individual cells vary across hemispheres and likely across individuals (Caron et al., 2013; Eichler et al., 2017; Honegger et al., 2011; Murthy et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the stochastic nature of KC wiring, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Associative learning mechanisms operate at KC output synapses in the mushroom body axonal lobes.
source: Associative learning mechanisms operate at KC output synapses, in the mushroom body axonal lobes, to re-weight KC outputs depending on experience and shift animal behavior (Cohn et al., 2015; Handler et al., 2019; Hige et al., 2015; Owald and Waddell, 2015).
evidence: This describes the location and function of learning mechanisms, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cerebellar granule cells have an average of four large, claw-shaped dendrites.
source: Cerebellar granule cells have an average of four large, claw-shaped dendrites that are innervated by clustered mossy fiber presynaptic sites in mossy fiber rosettes.
evidence: This provides comparative anatomical information about the vertebrate cerebellum.

claim: The similar convergence ratios in the cerebellum and mushroom body (4 or 5 sensory inputs per expansion layer cell) are thought to maximize dimensionality of sensory representations.
source: The similar convergence ratios in the cerebellum and mushroom body (4 or 5 sensory inputs, respectively, per expansion layer cell) are thought to maximize dimensionality of sensory representations by optimizing the tradeoff between stimulus representation, which is maximized when expansion layer neurons receive large combinations of inputs, and stimulus separation, which is maximized when expansion layer neurons receive few inputs (Albus, 1971; Cayco-Gajic et al., 2017; Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017; Marr, 1969).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about optimal coding supported by multiple citations.

claim: Four KC neuroblasts in each hemisphere produce approximately 500 KCs each.
source: In the fly, four KC neuroblasts in each hemisphere produce ~500 KCs each (Ito et al., 1997).
evidence: This provides quantitative information about KC neurogenesis supported by citation.

claim: Most neuroblasts pause their divisions for the first 8 hours after larval hatching, but KC neuroblasts continue to divide.
source: While most neuroblasts pause their divisions for the first 8 hr after larval hatching (ALH), the KC neuroblasts continue to divide; if larvae are fed the mitotic poison hydroxyurea (HU) during this time, KC neuroblasts can be specifically ablated (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994).
evidence: This describes the developmental timing that allows selective ablation, supported by citation.

claim: In animals lacking all KCs that receive olfactory inputs, olfactory learning is abrogated while innate olfactory behaviors are spared.
source: In these animals, lacking all KCs that receive olfactory inputs, olfactory learning is abrogated while innate olfactory behaviors are spared (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994).
evidence: This describes the behavioral consequences of KC ablation, supported by citation.

claim: lNB/BAlc is the only other neuroblast besides KC neuroblasts dividing from 0 to 8 hours after larval hatching and is thus susceptible to HU ablation.
source: Besides the KC neuroblasts, lNB/BAlc is the only other neuroblast in the fly central nervous system dividing from 0 to 8 hr ALH and is thus also susceptible to HU ablation (Das et al., 2013; Ito and Hotta, 1992; Lovick et al., 2016; Lovick and Hartenstein, 2015; Stocker et al., 1997; Sweeney et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the developmental timing that makes lNB/BAlc susceptible to HU, supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is a linear relationship between KC number and PN bouton number in HU-treated animals.
source: To ask if this corresponded to a decline in bouton number, we counted the number of PN boutons in each hemisphere (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2). This revealed a linear relationship between KC number and PN bouton number, suggesting that PNs reduce their population of boutons to match the KC population.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in figures.

claim: PNs reduce their population of boutons to match the KC population.
source: This revealed a linear relationship between KC number and PN bouton number, suggesting that PNs reduce their population of boutons to match the KC population.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the linear relationship observed in the data.

claim: The lateral horn appeared normal in HU-treated animals and its size did not correlate with KC number.
source: The lateral horn appeared normal in these animals and its size did not correlate with KC number, suggesting that PN projections to these two brain areas develop independent of one another (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: PN projections to the lateral horn and mushroom body calyx develop independent of one another.
source: The lateral horn appeared normal in these animals and its size did not correlate with KC number, suggesting that PN projections to these two brain areas develop independent of one another (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that lateral horn size is unaffected by KC loss.

claim: In animals with all four KC neuroblasts ablated, approximately 100 KCs remained.
source: We confirmed previous findings that in animals with all four KC neuroblasts ablated, the PNs fail to target the calyx and project only to the lateral horn (Stocker et al., 1997). In these animals, ~100 KCs remained (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with citation to previous work.

claim: The earliest-born KCs (γd KCs) receive visual and not olfactory input in adult flies.
source: Recently, these earliest-born cells, called γd KCs, have been shown to receive visual and not olfactory input in adult flies (Vogt et al., 2016; Yagi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: γd KCs receive olfactory inputs in the early larva and are sufficient for olfactory learning at that time.
source: Remarkably, these embryonic-born γd KCs receive olfactory inputs in the early larva and are sufficient for olfactory learning at that time (Eichler et al., 2017; Pauls et al., 2010); they must therefore switch their partner preferences across developmental stages.
evidence: This is supported by citations describing larval KC function.

claim: γd KCs switch their partner preferences across developmental stages.
source: Remarkably, these embryonic-born γd KCs receive olfactory inputs in the early larva and are sufficient for olfactory learning at that time (Eichler et al., 2017; Pauls et al., 2010); they must therefore switch their partner preferences across developmental stages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that γd KCs receive olfactory inputs in larvae but visual inputs in adults.

claim: Calyx size progressively decreases as KC number decreases in HU-treated animals.
source: We then examined calyx anatomy in animals with intermediate populations of KCs, likely derived from 1 to 3 remaining neuroblasts. We found a progressive decrease in the size of the mushroom body calyx in these animals as measured by the maximum cross-sectional area of the calyx (Figure 1B,C) or by calyx volume (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: The number of anterodorsal PNs was not reduced in animals with some or all KC neuroblasts ablated.
source: The number of anterodorsal PNs was not reduced in animals with some or all KC neuroblasts ablated, and the number of ventrolateral PNs was binary rather than graded, suggesting that vlPN number is determined by whether lNB/BAlc succumbed to HU, rather than by the KC complement (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: PN neurogenesis and survival do not require KC signals.
source: These results suggest that PN neurogenesis and survival do not require KC signals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PN numbers are not reduced when KCs are ablated.

claim: Individual PNs reduce their bouton production as the KC complement is reduced.
source: These results suggest that individual PNs do reduce their bouton production as the KC complement is reduced, and that this reduction is graded rather than binary (i.e. in animals with some but not all KC neuroblasts ablated, bouton number is in between 0 and the wild type number).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments examining individual PN bouton numbers in HU-treated animals.

claim: VM6 PN usually produces approximately 10 boutons in wild-type animals.
source: While VM6 usually produces ~10 boutons, we found only ~5 boutons in animals with reduced calyx size, and 0–1 bouton in animals with severe calyx reductions, likely lacking all olfactory KCs (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation of VM6 bouton number in control and manipulated animals.

claim: VM6 PN produces approximately 5 boutons in animals with reduced calyx size.
source: While VM6 usually produces ~10 boutons, we found only ~5 boutons in animals with reduced calyx size, and 0–1 bouton in animals with severe calyx reductions, likely lacking all olfactory KCs (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: There is no change in claw number on individual αβ KCs as the KC population is reduced.
source: Combining data from these two methods, we found no change in claw number on individual αβ KCs (Figure 2J–K) or γ KCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) as the KC population was reduced.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in figures.

claim: There is no change in claw number on individual γ KCs as the KC population is reduced.
source: Combining data from these two methods, we found no change in claw number on individual αβ KCs (Figure 2J–K) or γ KCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) as the KC population was reduced.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in figures.

claim: PNs reduce their bouton production on a cell-by-cell basis as the KC population shrinks, while KC claw number is unaffected by the size of the KC population.
source: From these experiments, we conclude that PNs reduce their bouton production on a cell-by-cell basis as the KC population shrinks, while KC claw number is unaffected by the size of the KC population (model, Figure 2L).
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: Expression of UAS-mud-RNAi using OK107-Gal4 produces potent amplification of KCs that is variable across animals, sometimes more than doubling KC number.
source: We observed potent amplification of KCs that was variable across animals, sometimes more than doubling KC number (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation of the effect of mud knockdown on KC number.

claim: PN bouton number doubled in mushroom bodies with the largest KC expansions.
source: We measured calyx size, which expanded dramatically, and used GH146-driven fluorescence to count PN bouton number, which doubled in mushroom bodies with the largest KC expansions (Figure 3C, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: PNs scale up their boutons when the KC population is expanded.
source: These results suggest that just as PNs scale down their boutons if the KC population is reduced, PNs scale up their boutons when the KC population is expanded.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that bouton number increases with KC expansion.

claim: There is no change in VM6 or MZ19+ cell numbers in brains with KC expansions.
source: First, we observed no change in VM6 or MZ19+ cell numbers in brains with KC expansions (Figure 3E,H), suggesting that PN numbers do not increase as KC number increases.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: PN numbers do not increase as KC number increases.
source: First, we observed no change in VM6 or MZ19+ cell numbers in brains with KC expansions (Figure 3E,H), suggesting that PN numbers do not increase as KC number increases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PN cell numbers remain constant despite KC expansion.

claim: There is no change in VM6 bouton numbers when KCs are expanded.
source: We observed no change in VM6 bouton numbers, perhaps because the VM6 PN already has a relatively large number of boutons (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with speculation about the reason.

claim: MZ19 cells increased their number of presynaptic boutons as the KC population expanded, from an average of 3.5 boutons per cell in controls to 4.75 boutons per cell in the KC-expansion genotype.
source: In contrast, MZ19 cells increased their number of presynaptic boutons as the KC population expanded, from an average of 3.5 boutons per cells in the control genotype to an average of 4.75 boutons per cell in the KC-expansion genotype.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental finding showing PN bouton increase with KC expansion.

claim: In brains with measurably enlarged calyces, MZ19+ boutons doubled.
source: In brains with measurably enlarged calyces, indicative of KC population expansion, MZ19+ boutons doubled (Figure 3D,F,G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: There is a slight increase in KC claw number from a median of 5 to 6 claws in animals with expanded KC complements.
source: Rather than a decrease in claw number per KC in animals with expanded KC complements, we found a slight increase in claw number, from a median of 5 to a median of 6 claws.
evidence: This is an experimental observation of KC claw numbers in KC-expansion animals.

claim: There is no change in α'β' KC claw number per cell in KC-expansion animals.
source: In these KCs of matched type, we found no change in KC claw number per cell, though we cannot rule out subtle differences.
evidence: This is an experimental observation for a specific KC type.

claim: In animals with an amplified KC complement, PNs dramatically increase their bouton production to match the KC population, while KCs may moderately increase, and do not reduce, their individual claw production.
source: Together, these experiments suggest that in animals with an amplified KC complement, PNs dramatically increase their bouton production to match the KC population, while KCs may moderately increase, and do not reduce, their individual claw production.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the KC expansion experiments.

claim: Knocking down mud in PN neuroblasts produced GH146-labeled PN complements of up to 600 cells, compared to approximately 120 GH146-labeled PNs in controls.
source: This strategy produced GH146-labeled PN complements of up to 600 cells, as compared to ~120 GH146-labeled PNs we counted in controls.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation of PN expansion.

claim: Ventrolateral PNs were much more susceptible to expansion than anterodorsal PNs when mud was knocked down in PN neuroblasts.
source: While the PN neuroblast Gal4 we used, 44F03, can label both lNB/BAlc and adNB/BAmv3 progeny (Awasaki et al., 2014), we found that ventrolateral PNs were much more susceptible to expansion than anterodorsal PNs.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with citation to the Gal4 line characterization.

claim: Supernumerary PNs innervated the antennal lobe, causing a massive expansion of antennal lobe area.
source: Supernumerary PNs innervated the antennal lobe, causing a massive expansion of antennal lobe area (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: There was no change in calyx area or total bouton number when PNs were expanded.
source: However, there was no change in calyx area or total bouton number in these animals compared to wild type (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: At a population level, the average number of boutons per PN was half that in controls when PNs were expanded.
source: At a population level, the average number of boutons per PN was half that in controls (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: PNs scale down their individual bouton repertoire to compensate for increases in the size of the PN population.
source: Thus PNs scale down their individual bouton repertoire to compensate for increases in the size of the PN population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that individual PN bouton numbers decrease when PN population increases.

claim: Driving DTA under control of VT033008 reduced the total PNs labeled by VT033008 and/or GH146 by nearly half.
source: Driving DTA under control of VT033008 reduced the total PNs labeled by VT033008 and/or GH146 by nearly half (Figure 5C), while VT033006>DTA reduced PNs labeled by VT03006 and/or GH146 by >90% (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation of PN ablation efficiency.

claim: VT033006>DTA reduced PNs labeled by VT033006 and/or GH146 by more than 90%.
source: Driving DTA under control of VT033008 reduced the total PNs labeled by VT033008 and/or GH146 by nearly half (Figure 5C), while VT033006>DTA reduced PNs labeled by VT03006 and/or GH146 by >90% (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is an experimental observation of PN ablation efficiency.

claim: For VT033008>DTA, loss of nearly half the PNs yielded no change in calyx area and a 20% reduction in overall bouton number.
source: For VT033008>DTA, loss of nearly half the PNs yielded no change in calyx area and a 20% reduction in overall bouton number (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in figures.

claim: While only approximately 10 PNs remain in VT033006>DTA animals (approximately 7% the normal complement), the number of boutons in the calyx was reduced by only half.
source: Remarkably, while we estimate that only ~10 PNs remain in VT033006>DTA animals (~7% the normal complement, Figure 5H), the number of boutons in the calyx was reduced by only half (Figure 5H,L).
evidence: This is an experimental observation showing dramatic PN bouton compensation.

claim: Individual PNs could have expanded their bouton production by as much as 6-fold in VT033006>DTA animals.
source: This suggests that individual PNs could have expanded their bouton production by as much as 6-fold.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the observed reduction in PN number and bouton number.

claim: At least 80% of KCs remained in VT033006>DTA brains with severe PN loss.
source: While we cannot rule out a small reduction in KC complement, at least 80% of KCs remained in these brains.
evidence: This is an experimental observation of KC survival after PN ablation.

claim: PN ablation brains had at least 85% as many KCs as control brains by flow cytometry.
source: We also subjected control and VT033006>DTA brains to flow cytometry and found that PN ablation brains had at least 85% as many KCs as did control brains (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation using flow cytometry to count KCs.

claim: Despite 90% reduction in the number of PNs and 50% reduction in their boutons, there was no reduction in claw number per KC in VT033006>DTA animals.
source: Surprisingly, despite 90% reduction in the number of PNs and 50% reduction in their boutons, we observed no reduction in claw number per KC.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding showing KC claw number is maintained despite severe PN loss.

claim: KCs are inflexible in their production of claws, even in the face of severe reduction of their typical, favored presynaptic partners.
source: Nevertheless, these data suggest that KCs are inflexible in their production of claws, even in the face of severe reduction of their typical, favored presynaptic partners.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that KC claw numbers remain constant despite severe PN reduction.

claim: PNs adjusted to changes in PN::KC ratio by altering their presynaptic boutons, while the distribution of KC claw numbers changed little.
source: The disparate and numerous strategies we used above to vary the ratio between PNs and KCs all produced the same result, that PNs adjusted to changes in PN::KC ratio by altering their presynaptic boutons, while the distribution of KC claw numbers changed little even when perturbations to PNs were so severe as to prevent production of the normal bouton complement.
evidence: This is a summary of the major finding across all experimental manipulations.

claim: Developmental mechanisms prioritize the sparseness of olfactory inputs to KCs.
source: This finding suggests that developmental mechanisms prioritize the sparseness of olfactory inputs to KCs, and might therefore preserve sparse odor coding and high-dimensional odor representations despite stark changes to the underlying circuit constituents.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the biological significance of the findings.

claim: Robust odor responses were observed in both sham-treated and HU-treated animals.
source: We observed robust odor responses in both conditions, with 8/28 sham-treated and 4/46 HU-treated calyces completely unresponsive.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from functional imaging experiments.

claim: A median of approximately 50% of cells from sham calyces responded to ethyl acetate and isobutyl acetate.
source: Using these criteria, a median of ~50% of cells from sham calyces responded to ethyl acetate and isobutyl acetate, and ~20–30% of cells to benzaldehyde and methylcyclohexanol (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation from functional imaging.

claim: A median of approximately 20-30% of cells from sham calyces responded to benzaldehyde and methylcyclohexanol.
source: Using these criteria, a median of ~50% of cells from sham calyces responded to ethyl acetate and isobutyl acetate, and ~20–30% of cells to benzaldehyde and methylcyclohexanol (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation from functional imaging.

claim: The proportions of KCs per calyx responding to each odor were statistically indistinguishable between sham and reduced-KC calyces.
source: We next compared the proportions of KCs per calyx responding to each odor between sham and reduced-KC calyces. These distributions were statistically indistinguishable (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of functional imaging data.

claim: In both sham and reduced-KC conditions, approximately 60% of cells responded to 0 or one odors.
source: Finally, we asked how many odors each cell responded to (Figure 7F). In each condition, ~60% of cells responded to 0 or one odors.
evidence: This is a quantitative experimental observation from functional imaging.

claim: Developmental plasticity mechanisms preserve qualitatively sparse KC odor responses when the KC population is experimentally reduced.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the developmental plasticity mechanisms operating to set the density of olfactory inputs to KCs preserve qualitatively sparse KC odor responses when the KC population is experimentally reduced.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional imaging experiments.

claim: The ratio between PNs and KCs in the larval olfactory circuit is starkly different from the adult: 21 embryonically-born PNs wire to early-born KCs to construct the larval mushroom body.
source: In keeping with this, the ratio between PNs and KCs in the larval olfactory circuit is starkly different from the adult: 21 embryonically-born PNs wire to early-born KCs to construct the larval mushroom body (Eichler et al., 2017; Masuda-Nakagawa et al., 2005; Ramaekers et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a comparison of developmental stages supported by citations.

claim: The 21 PNs in the early larva connect to approximately 75 KCs, a 1:3 ratio.
source: The 21 PNs in the early larva connect to ~75 KCs, a 1:3 ratio, while in the adult, ~150 PNs connect to ~2000 KCs, a 1:10 ratio. (Eichler et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of PN:KC ratios across developmental stages, supported by citations.

claim: In the adult, approximately 150 PNs connect to approximately 2000 KCs, a 1:10 ratio.
source: The 21 PNs in the early larva connect to ~75 KCs, a 1:3 ratio, while in the adult, ~150 PNs connect to ~2000 KCs, a 1:10 ratio. (Eichler et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of PN:KC ratios across developmental stages, supported by citations.

claim: PNs and KCs do not rely on each other for survival signals.
source: We found that unlike cells in many other systems, including the vertebrate cerebellum, PNs and KCs did not rely on each other for survival signals (Fan et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments showing PN and KC survival is independent, with citation to contrast with other systems.

claim: Setting connectivity density cell-autonomously in KCs could allow KCs to obtain the appropriate number of inputs at different life stages when cellular constituents are very different.
source: Instead, setting connectivity density cell-autonomously in KCs could allow KCs to obtain the appropriate number of inputs at the different life stages of the animal, when cellular constituents are very different from one another.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Approximately 10% of KCs are born after PN:KC synapsis has already initiated.
source: Similarly, while PN neurogenesis ceases well before PNs and KCs begin to contact one another in the pupa, we estimate that ~10% of KCs are born after PN:KC synapsis has already initiated (Muthukumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an estimate based on developmental timing, supported by citation.

claim: Strict, cell-autonomous dendrite structuring and flexible PN bouton production could together ensure that late-born KCs obtain the inputs appropriate to support coding.
source: Strict, cell-autonomous dendrite structuring and flexible PN bouton production could together ensure that late-born KCs obtain the inputs appropriate to support coding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how the developmental mechanisms support function.

claim: Olfactory PNs of different types are specified in a predictable temporal order.
source: Olfactory PNs of different types are specified in a predictable temporal order, have characteristic numbers of boutons, and overlap in their innervation of the calyx (Lai et al., 2008; Yu et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes established knowledge about PN development, supported by citations.

claim: Differences in bouton number across different PNs allow different odor channels to be differentially represented in the calyx and in KC odor responses.
source: Differences in bouton number across different PNs allow different odor channels to be differentially represented in the calyx and in KC odor responses (Caron et al., 2013; Honegger et al., 2011; Murthy et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the functional consequence of variable PN bouton numbers, supported by citations.

claim: Several classes of PNs differ in number between the sexes.
source: Several classes of PNs also differ in number between the sexes (Grabe et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes sexual dimorphism in PN populations, supported by citation.

claim: The spontaneous activity of different ORs correlates with number of boutons representing that odor channel in the calyx.
source: A recent analysis suggests that the spontaneous activity of different ORs correlates with number of boutons representing that odor channel in the calyx (Kennedy, 2019).
evidence: This is a recent finding from another study, supported by citation.

claim: KC number limits total bouton number across all PNs, while allocation of these boutons to individual PNs is determined by activity-based competition among PN types.
source: One possible model for how PNs scale to KC numbers while maintaining their relative representations in the calyx is thus that KC number limits total bouton number across all PNs, while allocation of these boutons to individual PNs is determined by activity-based competition among PN types.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the observations.

claim: Increasing the number of inputs per KC is theorized to reduce dimensionality of odor responses by making different KCs more similar to one another.
source: While increasing the number of inputs per KC is theorized to reduce dimensionality of odor responses by making different KCs more similar to one another, decreasing the number of inputs per KC is theorized to reduce dimensionality by reducing the number of different possible KC input combinations (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes theoretical predictions about coding, supported by citation.

claim: Decreasing the number of inputs per KC is theorized to reduce dimensionality by reducing the number of different possible KC input combinations.
source: While increasing the number of inputs per KC is theorized to reduce dimensionality of odor responses by making different KCs more similar to one another, decreasing the number of inputs per KC is theorized to reduce dimensionality by reducing the number of different possible KC input combinations (Litwin-Kumar et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes theoretical predictions about coding, supported by citation.

claim: The sweet spot maximizing dimensionality is approximately 5 inputs per KC.
source: That this sweet spot maximizing dimensionality, ~5 inputs per cell, is programmed into KC identity testifies to the evolutionary importance of maintaining connectivity density in associative brain centers that rely on combinatorial coding.
evidence: This is an interpretation combining theoretical predictions with experimental observations.

claim: The olfactory receptors are the largest insect gene family and have been subject to frequent and extreme gains and losses in many clades.
source: The olfactory receptors are the largest insect gene family and have been subject to frequent and extreme gains and losses in many clades.
evidence: This describes evolutionary patterns in olfactory receptor genes.

claim: Brain centers devoted to learning are radically different across species, as exemplified by the diversity in KC repertoire across arthropods.
source: Similarly, brain centers devoted to learning are radically different across species, as exemplified by the diversity in KC repertoire across arthropods (Strausfeld et al., 2009).

claim: Plastic development of PN presynaptic sites that makes room for additional players in the repertoire would allow immediate access of evolutionarily expanded PNs to the calyx and the use of their signals for olfactory learning.
source: Plastic development of PN presynaptic sites that makes room for additional players in the repertoire would allow immediate access of evolutionarily expanded PNs to the calyx and the use of their signals for olfactory learning, thus making time for the evolution of hardwired circuits for innate interpretations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the evolutionary significance of the findings.
